```
***
`if c then t else e` is notation for `ite c t e`, "if-then-else", which decides to
return `t` or `e` depending on whether `c` is true or false. The explicit argument
`c : Prop` does not have any actual computational content, but there is an additional
`[Decidable c]` argument synthesized by typeclass inference which actually
determines how to evaluate `c` to true or false. Write `if h : c then t else e`
instead for a "dependent if-then-else" `dite`, which allows `t`/`e` to use the fact
that `c` is true/false.

```
***
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.

```lean
Matrix.of.{v, u_2, u_3} {m : Type u_2} {n : Type u_3} {α : Type v} : (m → n → α) ≃ Matrix m n α
```
***
Cast a function into a matrix.

The two sides of the equivalence are definitionally equal types. We want to use an explicit cast
to distinguish the types because `Matrix` has different instances to pi types (such as `Pi.mul`,
which performs elementwise multiplication, vs `Matrix.mul`).

If you are defining a matrix, in terms of its entries, use `of (fun i j ↦ _)`. The
purpose of this approach is to ensure that terms of the form `(fun i j ↦ _) * (fun i j ↦ _)` do not
appear, as the type of `*` can be misleading.

Porting note: In Lean 3, it is also safe to use pattern matching in a definition as `| i j := _`,
which can only be unfolded when fully-applied. leanprover/lean4#2042 means this does not
(currently) work in Lean 4.

Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.

***
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.

```
***
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.

***
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.

***
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.

LinearMap.toMatrix₂.{u_1, u_5, u_6, u_9, u_10} {R : Type u_1} {M₁ : Type u_5} {M₂ : Type u_6} {n : Type u_9}
  {m : Type u_10} [CommSemiring R] [AddCommMonoid M₁] [Module R M₁] [AddCommMonoid M₂] [Module R M₂] [DecidableEq n]
  [Fintype n] [DecidableEq m] [Fintype m] (b₁ : Basis n R M₁) (b₂ : Basis m R M₂) :
  (M₁ →ₗ[R] M₂ →ₗ[R] R) ≃ₗ[R] Matrix n m R
```
***
`LinearMap.toMatrix₂ b₁ b₂` is the equivalence between `R`-bilinear forms on `M` and
`n`-by-`m` matrices with entries in `R`, if `b₁` and `b₂` are `R`-bases for `M₁` and `M₂`,
respectively.

```lean

```
***
The determinant of a matrix given by the Leibniz formula. 
***
*import Mathlib.LinearAlgebra.Matrix.Determinant.Basic*

```lean
LinearMap.SeparatingLeft.{u_1, u_2, u_3, u_5, u_6, u_7} {R : Type u_1} {R₁ : Type u_2} {R₂ : Type u_3} {M : Type u_5}
  {M₁ : Type u_6} {M₂ : Type u_7} [CommSemiring R] [AddCommMonoid M] [Module R M] [CommSemiring R₁] [AddCommMonoid M₁]
  [Module R₁ M₁] [CommSemiring R₂] [AddCommMonoid M₂] [Module R₂ M₂] {I₁ : R₁ →+* R} {I₂ : R₂ →+* R}
  (B : M₁ →ₛₗ[I₁] M₂ →ₛₗ[I₂] M) : Prop
```
***
A bilinear map is called left-separating if
the only element that is left-orthogonal to every other element is `0`; i.e.,
for every nonzero `x` in `M₁`, there exists `y` in `M₂` with `B x y ≠ 0`. 
***
*import Mathlib.LinearAlgebra.SesquilinearForm*

```lean
LinearMap.separatingLeft_iff_det_ne_zero.{u_2, u_5, u_13} {R₁ : Type u_2} {M₁ : Type u_5} {ι : Type u_13} [CommRing R₁]
  [AddCommMonoid M₁] [Module R₁ M₁] [DecidableEq ι] [Fintype ι] [IsDomain R₁] {B : M₁ →ₗ[R₁] M₁ →ₗ[R₁] R₁}
  (b : Basis ι R₁ M₁) : B.SeparatingLeft ↔ ((toMatrix₂ b b) B).det ≠ 0
```
